text.p: These are some of the main stories in Sofia newspapers today. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

-- The Marxist wing within the Socialist party demanded the exclusion of the former Socialist premier-designate Nikolai Dobrev from the party for bowing to opposition demands to give up the mandate and agree to early elections.
-- The outgoing cabinet raised petrol and diesel fuel prices by 48 percent on the average, in force from today.

-- Sofia mayor Stefan Sofianski was tipped at the most probable caretaker premier in the cabinet due to be appointed by the president, sources from the presidency said. The president's economic advisor Krassimir Angarski was the most likely to become finance minister in that cabinet.
-- The International Monetary Fund will resume talks om crucial aid to Bulgaria as soon as a caretaker government is in place, an IMF official said. @

-- Bulgaria's Association of Commercial Banks (ACB) said it would ask the central bank to lift its temporary ban on the use of part of banks' minimum required reserves as emergency refinancing to compensate deposit withdrawals, ACB officials said.

-- Bulgaria's chief prosecutor Ivan Tatarchev said criminal investigation might be launched against the outgoing Socialist premier Zhan Videnov, some of his ministers and officials from the Orion economic grouping for the economic collapse of the country. @
-- The ougoing cabinet is expected to discuss today a proposal of the state tobacco monopolist Bulgartabac Holding for a three-fold rise of prices of locally made cigarettes.
-- Socialist deputies will attend parliament sessions only when amendments to the Election Law are being debated, the Socialist parliamentary group decided.

-- Tens of thousands gathered in the centre of capital Sofia at a victory rally on Wednesday to celebrate the success of their month-long protests, after the socialist party gave up attempts to form a second government and elections were set for April. -- Sofia Newsroom, (++359-2) 981 8569
